Consequently, the claimed closed-form computation does not correctly implement the stated robustness measure.

The experimental tables contain serious inconsistencies. Moreover, Table 8 reports CPU/Banzhaf Spearman correlations of 0.87, -0.71, and 0.70 among three rankings. A Taylor expansion around zero provides no uniform approximation guarantee over the coalition utilities actually encountered, and no ranking-margin analysis bounds induced ordering errors. For example, the F1 surrogate becomes twice recall, discarding prediction-rate dependence. Small empirical discordance on two metrics cannot justify replacing general linear-fractional utilities by the exact semivalue equality written in Section 3.

The robustness measure does not adequately represent the motivating utility choices. It averages uniformly over the entire circle, including negative combinations, while convex trade-offs occupy only a quadrant and candidate classification metrics occupy selected directions. The analytical explanation for Banzhaf relies on an unverified assumption that marginal-contribution vectors at different coalition sizes have zero covariance. Appendix B.7 additionally drops within-utility cross-size covariance terms from its variance expressions, although the explicitly stated cross-utility assumption does not imply their disappearance. The evaluation uses tiny tabular subsets and one logistic-regression learner. Five Monte Carlo repetitions assess sampling variation rather than robustness across dataset splits. There are no utility-trade-off experiments or downstream top-k selection and retraining evaluations, and the added practical value over direct ranking comparisons remains unestablished.
